newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan independence movement losing steam.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan independence movement losing steam.

text.p: Ten years ago, Taiwan people united under a passionate cry for independence and hailed as heroes those who boldly challenged the Nationalist government's goal of reuniting the island with estranged rival China.

Today, with Taiwan acutely isolated by a sometimes-bullying communist China, the so-called "Taiwan independence movement" is in danger of becoming obsolete and politicians once identified with it are scrambling to find a more populist platform.
Solidarity is gone and independence activists now squabble over just exactly what they are fighting for.
Stalwart independence advocates, praised not so long ago as freedom fighters, are branded as extremist, dangerous elements that threaten the island's fundamental political stability.

So drastic is the change in attitude that Taiwan's largest opposition party, which defied martial law in the 1980s in its almost religious zeal for independence and legal status, has virtually abandoned the platform as a political liability.
"The Taiwan independence movement is at a crossroads. Where is it going from here?" said Lu Ya-li, a political science professor at National Taiwan University.
"The issue is slowly being marginalised. It no longer incites people's passion nor garners emotional support. Instead, it scares people who just want stability," he said.
Polls regularly show that less than one in five of Taiwan's 21 million people want to pursue a final divorce from China.
About half prefer things the way they are -- an ambiguous balance in which China tolerates Taiwan's de facto independence but threatens force to thwart a declaration of sovereignty.
Taiwan and China have been ruled separately since a Chinese civil war split them in 1949, sending the defeated Nationalists into U.S.-supported exile on the island southeast of Shanghai.
Both say they want to unify, but disagree sharply on how.
Political experts cite two fundamental reasons for the loss of passion for independence -- Taiwan's democratic renaissance and communist China's military coercion.

Even the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, whose fight for the right to advocate independence helped bring down martial law in 1987, said the independence issue is out of date now that Taiwan has become a full-fledged democracy. "Ten years ago, the Taiwan independence movement was very important because Taiwan was not an independent country. It was ruled by the Nationalists who came from China," party chairman Hsu Hsin-liang told Reuters in a recent interview.

"Although the Nationalists are still in power, they have gone through the democratic election process and are no longer an outside government. Taiwan is already independent, so there is no need to argue the issue anymore," he said.

Pressured by fervent dissenters, the exiled Republic of China phased in democratic reforms in the 1980s that culminated in the first direct election of a Chinese president last March. The poll gave incumbent Lee Teng-hui his first popular mandate.

But China, suspecting Lee of covertly pursuing independence despite his stated wish to reunify, launched months of war games near the island before the election to dissuade voters from supporting pro-independence candidates.
Beijing's military intimidation began soon after Lee managed to make a private, but high-profile U.S. visit in mid-1995 -- a move China denounced as the work of a splittist provocateur.
Even Taiwan's most renowned independence activist, the Democratic Progressive Party's 1996 presidential candidate Peng Ming-min, admitted independence has become a difficult sell.
"People do become complacent over time and some would rather have stability than something which they fear would threaten their security," Peng said in a recent interview.
"But a political party should not just go along with what the average person wants. It should stand up for what is right and educate the people," the 72-year-old Peng insisted.
A dissident who spent 23 years in exile under martial law, Peng openly attacks the softening stance of his own party, branding it a "satellite" of the Nationalists.

Some diehard activists abandoned their support of the Democratic Progressive Party and formed a new Taiwan Independence Party in October to keep alive their ideal of a drive toward sovereignty. But a recent publicity campaign by the new party has stirred little public enthusiasm.

"A lot of us who have been supporters of the Democratic Progressive Party became disillusioned and wanted to form a party that would remain genuine to the cause," party chairman Lee Chen-yuan told Reuters.

Taiwan Independence Party leaders were enraged after Democratic Progressive Party chief Hsu told Reuters in November that U.N. membership was "impossible" due to China's objections and that Taipei should not risk provoking Beijing.
"Those comments show a complete loss of ideals and lack of understanding from Hsu concerning the Taiwan independence principle," Lee said.
Hsu said the newly formed party, by ignoring reality, would remain a small interest group marginalised from the mainstream.
"The fact is, Taiwan needs support from foreign countries in order to gain greater recognition of its sovereignty, and right now no country wants us to provoke China," Hsu said.
"People in Taiwan, like people anywhere, want stability and prosperity. The only parties that will be legitimate are those that are able to reflect mainstream values in changing times."
